title: Hosted API demo - Chat & text generation basics
summary: Redwood AE + SE walked Greenfield through the Hosted API for chat/text generation. Covered streaming responses, key request parameters (temperature, max_tokens, stop sequences), retry/idempotency best practices, and how to instrument retries. Customer is evaluating for a pilot focused on customer support summarization with a timeline of end of Q4. Next steps: share pricing, security docs, run a short benchmark with sample prompts.

transcript:
Header:
- Date: 2026-11-01
- Time: 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~45 minutes
- Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonas Kim (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (CTO - Greenfield), Sana Mirza (ML Eng), Evelyn Rios (Product)

Summary:
Maya: quick agenda, we'll demo the hosted API for chat and text generation basics, then go into streaming, params, and retries, and leave time for Q&A.

Topics: streaming, params, retries/idempotency, console walk, benchmark.

00:00 Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, is this time still good for you?
00:05 Liam: yep, all good from our side, thanks.
00:09 Jonas: quick intro, i'm jonas, i'm the se on the account, i'll jump into the console and the streaming bits.
00:18 Evelyn: great, want to focus on latency and cost, our main constraint is 200ms p50 for short replies, and cost per session is also important.
00:30 Maya: perfect; so greenfield is using an in-house microservice today and evaluating hosted APIs to replace it?
00:36 Liam: correct - we have a home-grown model pipeline but infra ops are getting heavy, might offload to hosted for some routes.
00:44 Sana: our prompts are a mix of retrieval-augmented and few-shot templates, fairly consistent length, typically 100-400 tokens.
00:52 Jonas: ok good, that matches a lot of customers. i'll start with the hosted api basics — how we do chat generative calls, streaming, params like temperature/max_tokens, and then retries.
01:05 Jonas: when you call the /v1/chat/completions endpoint you can stream responses back so you get partial tokens as they generate; we support SSE and websocket styles (note: docs show SSE example).
01:20 Jonas: streaming helps a lot for perceived latency because you can render partial text while the model finishes. for your p50 SLA that can shave off 200-300ms in UI.
01:33 Sana: is streaming enabled by default?
01:36 Jonas: it's optional. you set stream=true and then you get chunks. if stream is false you'll get the full response at once.
01:45 Maya: quick note — some customers use streaming + smaller max_tokens per chunk to reduce latency for long responses.
01:52 Jonas: now parameters: temperature controls randomness; top_p is nucleus sampling. we generally recommend starting with temp=0.2 for deterministic support answers, or 0.0 if you want near-exact retrieval.
02:07 Jonas: max_tokens controls max generation length; combined with stop sequences you can control truncation. stop is handy for multi-turn templates to prevent the model repeating system tokens.
02:18 Evelyn: ok, and what about top_k or presence/frequency penalties?
02:22 Jonas: we expose frequency and presence penalty; they help reduce repetition. top_k isn't exposed in the hosted defaults but top_p covers most use cases.
02:32 Liam: curious about deterministic behavior for safety-critical responses — do you suggest temp=0?
02:36 Jonas: temp=0 is the most deterministic but not truly deterministic across model versions; pinning model version and doing unit tests (eval prompts) is recommended.
02:46 Sana: how do we handle timeouts and retries? our current infra retries idempotently but some of our calls are not idempotent.
02:53 Jonas: good question. we recommend an idempotency key header for POST-style inference to safely retry. Redwood's hosted API returns a request_id and you can replay with same idempotency key.
03:06 Jonas: retries should be exponential backoff + jitter; avoid retrying on 4xx except rate-limit headers. on 5xx or network errors do a limited retry.
03:18 Maya: we also recommend application-level dedupe using the request_id to avoid duplicated visible outputs to end users.
03:25 Sana: does the SDK manage idempotency automatically?
03:28 Jonas: our SDKs include helpers; they set a client-side UUID if you don't provide one, and they expose retry policies you can override.
03:36 Jonas: another nuance — streaming + retries: if the connection drops mid-stream, you can resume by reissuing with same idempotency key; runtime will dedupe tokens up to the last confirmed chunk but this is limited, better to checkpoint at logical boundaries.
03:52 Evelyn: any recommended patterns for long-running assistant sessions?
03:56 Jonas: for long context keep the last N turns in context and store embeddings for retrieval; use prefix caching for repeated prefixes which we support on the runtime to cut tokens.
04:06 Liam: you mentioned caching — is that on the hosted side or do we need to implement?
04:10 Jonas: Redwood offers automatic prefix/KV caching for common prompts on Dedicated; on Hosted we have response cache options for recent identical requests and CDN-level caching for embeddings depending on keys and TTL.
04:22 Sana: ok good. what about streaming delivery protocols — do you recommend SSE vs websocket?
04:26 Jonas: SSE is simpler to integrate in most web clients, web sockets give more control for bi-directional comms. both work; SSE is generally fine for UI streaming text.
04:36 Maya: i want to show the console briefly — quick tour of usage dashboard, streaming logs, and retry traces.
04:42 Jonas: opening the console share screen now, bear with me — loading.. (screen share audio)
05:00 Jonas: in the console you can see per-route latency, tokens consumed, and a trace of requests including the request_id and any retries.
05:12 Jonas: here's an example trace where a retry was triggered due to a transient 502, you'll see the retry attempts and the final success.
05:23 Sana: can we get logs shipped to our SIEM?
05:26 Jonas: yes, we support event export to customer-owned cloud storage and integrations with common SIEMs; we can include request metadata and audit trails.
05:37 Liam: security stuff — SAML SSO, SCIM, SOC2. are those included?
05:41 Maya: yes, SOC2 and SSO via SAML/OIDC are available for enterprise plans; we can share the security pack after this call.
05:51 Sana: data residency — can you keep data in eu-west?
05:54 Jonas: hosted API supports regional routing; depending on plan we can pin to EU regions and apply data retention policies.
06:05 Evelyn: ok great. back to params — any tips for cost control?
06:10 Jonas: control max_tokens, use stop sequences, and use caching/prefix caching where possible. batching at the client side for embeddings is another lever. our Optimize product can give suggestions per-route.
06:23 Maya: also note model selection — smaller quantized models can be cheaper; we show cost-per-token in the console so you can compare.
06:32 Liam: do you have autoscaling or reserved capacity for pilots?
06:35 Maya: yes, Dedicated/reserved capacity is an option for predictable throughput; for pilot hosted with free credits usually works but we can evaluate when you need throughput guarantees.
06:47 Jonas: quick demo snippet for streaming: (describes SSE flow) client opens stream, sends request with stream=true, runtime returns chunks with incremental tokens and final event. watch the request_id header.
06:59 Sana: is there a size limit on stream chunks?
07:02 Jonas: chunks are small; single tokens or token groups; large payloads are split. you shouldn't see more than a few KB per chunk typically.
07:12 Evelyn: what about rate limits?
07:15 Jonas: hosted has per-account rate limits, per-route throttles, and token rate quotas; the console shows your current quota and we expose headers returning X-RateLimit-Remaining.
07:26 Liam: if we hit a rate limit mid-session, what's the recommended UX?
07:30 Jonas: return a polite retry-after to user and fall back to a cached answer if available; for critical flows you can route to a smaller cheaper model as a graceful degradation.
07:41 Sana: any gotchas with stop sequences across different models?
07:44 Jonas: stop sequences are respected by most models but behavior can vary; test on your prompt set and set a conservative max_tokens.
07:53 Maya: ok, i'll share a sample prompt set and a short benchmark plan — jonas will run a hosted run for 1k messages using your prompts to measure p50/p95 and cost.
08:04 Jonas: i'll also capture streaming latency vs full response to give you numbers.
08:09 Liam: timeline?
08:11 Maya: we'll aim for results by 2026-11-10 and a follow-up call week of 2026-11-09 or 11-16 depending on your availability.
08:20 Sana: can you also show an example of exponential backoff implementation?
08:23 Jonas: sure — typical pattern: initial delay 200ms, then multiply by 2 with jitter, max 3 retries; respect Retry-After header. avoid retrying on permanent errors.
08:35 Evelyn: fine, for our product we need a small spec to hand to eng — can you send a one-pager with recommended client settings?
08:41 Maya: yes, we'll include recommended temp, top_p, max_tokens, stop, idempotency header sample, and retry pattern.
08:48 Liam: any pricing rough numbers for pilot?
08:50 Maya: i'll send a pilot pricing sheet; for hosted small pilots we usually estimate per-token cost and give volume tiers — details outbound.
08:58 Sana: about instrumentation, do you surface token-level cost per request in the console?
09:02 Jonas: yes, per-request token and cost breakdown per model, plus aggregated cost per route.
09:10 Evelyn: one more question — what's the typical time to provision a trial key?
09:13 Maya: immediate via console for self-serve, with rate limits; if you need higher quotas we do a quick request and can upgrade within 1-2 business days.
09:21 Liam: ok that's helpful.
09:24 Maya: closing Q&A, any other concerns?
09:27 Sana: just to confirm, SDKs have examples for streaming and idempotency?
09:31 Jonas: yes, node/python/sdk examples in the docs and sample repo.
09:36 Evelyn: looks good.
09:38 Maya: recap of next steps — i'll send pricing + quickstart + security pack; jonas will run the benchmark; sana will send prompt set; schedule follow-up after results.
09:51 Liam: thanks everyone, appreciate it.
09:53 Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up.

Notes / Links shared:
- Quickstart repo: https://redwood.example/quickstart (will include in follow-up)
- Security pack / SOC2: link to be sent

End of call.
